Article Title: Air India Phuket-Delhi incident: All 3 hydraulic systems failed; pilot tested positive for psychoactive substance
Article Text:
The hydraulic failure itself, the more immediate cause of the injuries onboard, unfolded within a five-second window. VT-EXO, an eight-year-old A320neo carrying 145 people, had just been cleared to climb from FL340 to FL360 after entering Kolkata Flight Information Region.

MUMBAI: The preliminary investigation into the August 4 Air India Phuket-Delhi accident has found that the aircraft's three hydraulic systems, green, blue and yellow, lost pressure within seconds while the A320 was cruising at 36,000 feet, triggering an autopilot disengagement, stall warning and an altitude upset. Alongside the technical findings, the Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau (AAIB) has recommended that the DGCA take action against the Pilot-in-Command, who tested non-negative for psychoactive substance use following the flight."The confirmation of use of psycho-active substance is a serious concern, and AAIB recommends appropriate actions by DGCA on priority," the report said. The interim safety recommendation asked the regulator to "take appropriate actions as deemed fit to prevent abuse of psycho-active substance." Post-flight, both pilots underwent a breath analyser test, which came back satisfactory. But the subsequent psychoactive substance detection test returned a non-negative result for the PIC, a finding confirmed by a follow-up laboratory blood test. The co-pilot tested negative on both counts.The hydraulic failure itself, the more immediate cause of the injuries onboard, unfolded within a five-second window.VT-EXO, an eight-year-old A320neo carrying 145 people, had just been cleared to climb from FL340 to FL360 after entering Kolkata Flight Information Region. At 04:02:43 UTC, the flight control system "detected loss of green hydraulic system." Four seconds later, the flight control (F/CTL) system detected loss of Blue and Yellow hydraulic systems. With all three systems compromised simultaneously, the autopilot disengaged, a continuous repetitive chime sounded, and the stall warning triggered for two seconds. The aircraft "encountered altitude upset," gaining 372 feet before falling 292 feet from its assigned level, the report said.The co-pilot, who was Pilot Flying, responded first to the upset before the captain took over the controls. Recovery was swift. "At around 04:02:52 UTC, the Blue hydraulic system was recovered, and a few seconds later, the Yellow hydraulic and the Green hydraulic systems were also recovered," the report said. It restored normal flight control surfaces within seconds of the failure.But with seatbelt signs off during cruise, the sudden upset threw passengers and crew around the cabin. Twenty-four people, including four cabin crew, needed medical attention on landing; four were hospitalised with serious injuries. The cabin damage was extensive: cracked ceiling panels across multiple rows, dislodged overhead bins, a broken emergency exit handle, a lavatory commode "uprooted from its original location," and a bent crew seat. Despite the injuries, the flight crew chose not to divert, opting instead to continue to Delhi while requesting medical priority from ATC. The aircraft landed safely on runway 11L at 05:30 UTC, around ninety minutes after the failure.Investigators have already flagged one detail for closer scrutiny: the aircraft was dispatched from Phuket under an active Minimum Equipment List item for the Power Transfer Unit, invoked a week earlier on July 28. The PTU serves as an auxiliary hydraulic source shared between the green and yellow systems, and its status at the time of the failure is expected to be a focus of the ongoing probe. Flight recorder data has been downloaded and is under analysis, and a technical team from Airbus and France's BEA inspected the aircraft in Delhi in mid-August, after which hydraulic components and fluid samples were removed for further testing.“The Airbus A320 aircraft has three hydraulic systems. They are identified as the green, blue and yellow systems. Together they supply hydraulic power at 3000 psi (206 bar) to the main power users. Services which are not used during flight are isolated from the main supply. Hydraulic fluid cannot be transferred from one system to another. Each system has its own hydraulic reservoir,” the report said, explaining the hydraulics on the aircraft.On the green system, the normal source of pressure is the Engine Driven Pump (EDP) located on the left engine and, as an auxiliary source, the Power Transfer Unit (PTU). On the blue system, the normal source of pressure is the electrical pump (E-Pump) and, as an auxiliary source, the Ram Air Turbine (RAT). On the yellow system, the normal source of pressure is the EDP located on the right engine and as auxiliary sources the PTU and the electric pump (E-Pump). “Each hydraulic system pressurisation information is available for the aircraft systems through one pressure transmitter (numerical value of the pressure), two pressure switches (discrete value indicating if there is a loss of pressure). Relevant Hydraulic components were removed from the aircraft for further analysis,” the report said. The PTU is an auxiliary pressure supply for either the green or yellow systems without transfer of fluid between the two systems. It operates automatically if there is a delta pressure of 500 psi between the green/yellow or yellow/green hydraulic systems, it addedThe said report is preliminary, and a detailed technical investigation is still underway.
Article Summary: Preliminary investigation into the August 4 Air India Phuket-Delhi accident has found that the aircraft's three hydraulic systems, green, blue and yellow, lost pressure within seconds while the A320 was cruising at 36,000 feet. Autopilot disengaged, a continuous repetitive chime sounded, and the stall warning triggered for two seconds. The aircraft "encountered altitude upset," gaining 372 feet before falling 292 feet.

Article Title: 'Why should I even respond to this?': Aaditya Thackeray on Disha Salian case after HC orders CBI probe
Article Text:
Bombay HC orders

CBI probe

NEW DELHI: Shiv Sena (UBT) leader Aaditya Thackeray on Thursday dismissed allegations linking him to the death of celebrity manager Disha Salian, questioning why he should respond to them. His remarks came after the Bombay high court directed the CBI to probe Salian’s death.Speaking to reporters, Aaditya Thackeray, the son of former Maharashtra chief minister Uddhav Thackeray said, "It's something that I have nothing to do about and not even thought about. Why should I even respond to this? BJP tries to defame everybody. They have tried to make Rahul Gandhi a 'Pappu' for years.”“They have tried to defame me for the last six years. Anybody who pricks the BJP, they have a problem with them. Like I said, when you have nothing to do with anything, why speak on anything or give it any importance? That's my stand..." he added.Earlier in the day, Maharashtra minister Nitesh Rane said that if Thackeray and others named in connection with the case had nothing to do with Salian’s death, they should come forward and clarify their position.Rane said he had maintained from the beginning that Salian’s death should not be treated as a suicide and expressed confidence that the CBI investigation would establish the facts."We were clear from day one that this was not a suicide; this was a murder case.And events of that nature are now coming to light. Now the CBI investigation will begin, and an FIR will be lodged," Rane said.He said he expected the probe to examine allegations of evidence being destroyed and misuse of power."My only expectation is that regarding the wrong that was done to our sister named Disha Salian—the way power was misused to destroy evidence and proof—all of those things are now going to come out. In the end, no matter how much you try to hide the truth, it eventually comes out," he added.The remarks came after the Bombay high court directed the CBI to register an FIR and conduct a thorough investigation into the circumstances surrounding Salian’s death. The court also directed Malvani Police Station to hand over relevant records to the CBI.The high court said no person should be treated as an accused merely on the basis of allegations made before the court.“Nobody shall be treated as an accused unless in the opinion of the investigating officer there are sufficient grounds to raise reasonable suspicion against him depending on the material collected during the investigation,” the court said.The CBI has been asked to appoint a suitably experienced and senior officer to conduct the investigation.The court also said that if the probe finds that no criminal case has been made out, the CBI must file an appropriate summary report before the competent court.“In case the investigation reveals that no case is made out, then the CBI shall file the appropriate summary report before the court concerned,” it said.Salian’s father, Satish Salian, would be free to challenge such a report and file objections before the court.The high court had earlier raised concerns over the registration of only an Accidental Death Report (ADR), instead of an FIR, despite allegations made by Salian’s family. It also noted that copies of the post-mortem report and ADR had not been provided to the family even years after her death.Advocate Nilesh Ojha, who represented Satish Salian, said the court had directed the CBI to record his statement and appoint a senior officer to investigate the case.The court described Salian’s father as an “unfortunate” parent who had lost his young daughter in “tragic circumstances” and said the matter required a substantive investigation. However, it did not make any adverse finding against any individual named in the allegations.Thackeray had separately approached the high court seeking to intervene in the proceedings. In his application, he described Satish Salian’s petition as “false, frivolous and motivated” and sought an opportunity to be heard before any order was passed.Salian, a celebrity manager, was found dead on June 8, 2020, after falling from a building in Mumbai. Her death occurred days before actor Sushant Singh Rajput was found dead at his Bandra residence.
Article Summary: Aaditya Thackeray dismisses allegations linking him to death of celebrity manager Disha Salian. His remarks came after the Bombay high court directed the CBI to probe Salian’s death. Maharashtra minister Nitesh Rane said that if Thackery and others named in connection with the case had nothing to do with Salian's death, they should come forward.

JAMMU: A joint team of security forces discovered a terrorist hideout and seized a cache of arms and ammunition during a search operation in Mahore tehsil in J&K’s Reasi district on Thursday.Based on inputs from the local Army intelligence unit, a joint team of the Army’s 58 Rashtriya Rifles and J&K Police’s Special Operations Group launched an anti-terror operation in the forested Khataji Ridge area. After intensive combing of the tough terrain, the search party busted a hideout, officials said.The recovery included 140 AK-47 rounds, an AK magazine, 19 PIKA LMG (Light Machine Gun) rounds, 25 rounds of 9mm pistol, one pistol, a grenade, medicines and six cassettes.Multiple cordon-and-search operations have been carried out in the hilly districts of Doda, Kishtwar, Kathua, Rajouri, Poonch, Ramban, Udhampur, and Reasi — all in Jammu division — recently, following inputs about the movement of terror suspects in the region’s higher reaches.

NEW DELHI: An IndiGo flight operating from Doha to Bengaluru (6E 1302) was diverted to Muscat after the pilot-in-command (PIC) fell ill. An emergency was declared and the aircraft landed in Muscat. The airline is sending another aircraft to Muscat to fly passengers to their destination. The PIC has received medical care and has recovered."IndiGo flight 6E 1302, operating from Doha to Bengaluru on Sept 3, 2026 was diverted to Muscat due to an urgent requirement of medical attention for one of the operating crew members. We regret the inconvenience caused to our customers and are making all efforts to minimise it, including offering refreshments and timely updates as they wait for the aircraft at Muscat. The safety of our customers, crew, and aircraft remains our top priority at IndiGo,” the spokesperson added.

Article Title: Inspiring story on leadership: "I always define leadership as: do you care about your teammates...and do you care what we're trying to accomplish"- How Tom Brady led teams to greatness
Article Text:
Tom Brady (Getty Images)

Tom Brady’s leadership philosophy was built around caring

PBD Podcast

2023

“Tom Brady on the Art of Leading Teammates,”

When and where Tom Brady shared the leadership message

caring about the other person and collectively caring about what the group was trying to achieve

Tom Brady learned team-first leadership at Michigan

University of Michigan

How Brady put his leadership philosophy into practice

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Tom Brady spent more than two decades being judged by rings, records and unforgettable performances. Yet when he talks about leadership, his definition reaches far beyond statistics. In a discussion about motivating teammates, Brady explained why genuine care, trust and a shared purpose shaped the way he led. His words offer a revealing look at the mindset behind one of football's most successful careers.Brady's approach to leadership was not simply about demanding more from the players around him. He believed a leader first had to build a relationship with the people he expected to follow him.During the, Brady discussed his leadership style and what helped him motivate teammates. The conversation, published in, turned toward leadership, when host Patrick Bet-David asked Brady about the methods he used to drive his players.Brady's answer centered on one word: caring.He explained that the relationship between a leader and teammates cannot be purely transactional. Players need to believe that the person beside them genuinely cares about them and about the goal they are pursuing together.That idea also appears in Brady's later Harvard Business Review work, where he expanded on his definition of team leadership. The article,was published in 2024 and explored seven principles he believed helped leaders bring out the best in teammates.The quote at the center of this discussion captures that philosophy:“I always define leadership as, do you care about your teammates or coworkers, and do you care what we’re trying to accomplish?” Brady. “That, to me, is great leadership. And there are a lot of people that go about those in different ways.”The wording is powerful because Brady does not begin with authority, experience or talent. He begins with people.For him, leadership starts with asking whether teammates know they matter and whether everyone remains committed to the same objective.The quote has circulated online in shortened form, but its underlying idea is supported by Brady's own extended comments.In the 2023 PBD Podcast conversation, Brady said his view of relationships in a team environment came down to. He argued that trust develops when people know their leader genuinely cares about them.That conversation gives important context to the quote. Brady was not describing leadership as a motivational speech or a title attached to a job. He was talking about the daily relationship between teammates.He also stressed the importance of vulnerability and mutual trust. In his view, players had to feel comfortable relying on one another. That trust could not be manufactured simply because someone was the quarterback or captain.Brady's later HBR article developed the same philosophy in greater detail. He wrote that leadership comes down to caring about teammates and caring about winning together. He connected that belief to trust, arguing that people are more willing to give their best when they feel valued by those around them.Brady traced much of his team-first mindset back to his time at theHis college career did not follow the straightforward path often associated with a future NFL superstar. He redshirted as a freshman and later found himself behind other quarterbacks on the depth chart. Yet those setbacks became part of his leadership education.In his HBR article, Brady recalled competing with Brian Griese for the starting quarterback position. Griese won the job, and Brady said his role was to support and challenge him in practice rather than undermine him. Michigan went undefeated that season and won the national championship.That experience reinforced a lesson that stayed with him.Individual recognition was not the ultimate prize. Winning as a group mattered more.Brady later described this mindset through an old sports question: whether someone wants to be a star or a champion. For him, the answer was clear. He wanted to contribute to something bigger than himself.That attitude became especially important during his NFL career. As a quarterback, Brady naturally occupied one of the most visible positions on the field. Every touchdown, mistake and major decision could draw attention to him.But he repeatedly emphasized the people around him.Brady's definition of leadership becomes more meaningful when paired with the examples he gave from his playing career.At Tampa Bay, he noticed that screen plays were producing poor results because offensive linemen were missing blocks. Rather than simply criticizing them, Brady created his own incentive. He promised to pay each offensive lineman $1,000 whenever a screen play gained more than 15 yards.The money was not necessarily the main point. Brady believed the gesture showed appreciation and made the linemen feel involved in the outcome.He also spoke about recognizing people whose contributions were less visible. Football teams rely on trainers, equipment staff, meal workers and many others whose names rarely appear in headlines.Brady believed leaders should make those people feel valued too.His approach also involved holding teammates accountable. Because he worked to establish trust, he felt he could challenge players directly without making them feel personally attacked. That balance between support and honesty became another important part of his leadership style.Perhaps that is what makes Brady's words resonate beyond football.A quarterback can throw a perfect pass, but he cannot win alone. A business executive can set a strategy, but employees still have to believe in it. A coach can design a game plan, but players have to trust one another enough to execute it.Brady's message is therefore much bigger than his NFL career.Leadership, in his view, is not about standing above everyone else. It is about standing with them, understanding what they need and making sure everyone remains connected to the same goal.That is why his simple question carries so much weight: Do you care about your teammates, and do you care about what you are trying to accomplish together?For a player who spent his career chasing championships, Brady's answer offers a different definition of what it means to win. The scoreboard may measure the final result, but the relationships built along the way can determine whether a team ever gets there in the first place.
Article Summary: Tom Brady’s leadership philosophy was built around caring. Brady's approach to leadership was not simply about demanding more from the players around him. He believed a leader first had to build a relationship with the people he expected to follow him. For him, leadership starts with asking whether teammates know they matter.

Article Title: "We lost a baby": Erin Andrews breaks down over devastating pregnancy loss as she shares the emotional toll of trying for another baby
Article Text:
Erin Andrews (Getty Images)

Erin Andrews opens up about pregnancy loss and guilt

Call Her Daddy

Erin Andrews and Jarret Stoll remain hopeful about growing their family

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Erin Andrews has opened up about a deeply personal loss that remains difficult to discuss. The FOX Sports reporter revealed that she and her husband, former NHL player Jarret Stoll, lost a pregnancy while trying to have another child. Speaking about the experience, Andrews described the guilt she has carried, even though the loss was beyond her control. Her candid admission offers a glimpse into the emotional side of their long journey to expand their family.For Andrews, the dream of having another child has come with years of uncertainty, difficult decisions and painful setbacks. She and Stoll welcomed their son, Mack, in June 2023 after turning to surrogacy following a long fertility journey.During an appearance on Alex Cooper’spodcast, Andrews spoke about the pregnancy loss and the emotions that followed. She said the couple had moved into a larger home because they expected to welcome another baby. When that pregnancy ended, the new space became an unexpected reminder of what they had hoped for.“I mean, there’s a lot of guilt on my end. You feel like a failure. You know, we just moved into this new house.It’s a lot bigger than what we had before because we thought we were having another baby. We lost a baby last year. And then you’re like, ‘Why are we doing this, ’cause we don’t have the second?'” Andrews said during an appearance on Alex Cooper’s Call Her Daddy podcast.The loss followed an earlier chapter marked by fertility challenges. Andrews was diagnosed with cervical cancer in 2016, and doctors advised her to freeze her embryos before treatment. She and Stoll subsequently went through nine rounds of IVF before choosing surrogacy.Their first surrogate pregnancy was also unsuccessful. A later attempt eventually led to the birth of Mack, making his arrival an especially meaningful moment for the couple.Andrews has made it clear that the couple's hopes for another child have not disappeared. She has continued to explore her options, including another IVF attempt in 2026, despite previous disappointments.Through those experiences, Stoll has remained a source of support. Andrews previously praised how he stood beside her during cancer treatment and the fertility process.“My husband was so amazing about learning about my cancer. He was so amazing about supporting me any way he could with either the shots, the transfers, the retrievals. Not a lot of guys understand all that,” Andrews said.The couple's experience also highlights how complicated the road to parenthood can become after years of fertility treatment. For Andrews, however, the story is not defined only by loss.She continues to balance motherhood, marriage and a demanding broadcasting career while leaving the door open for another child. The hope remains, even after everything the couple has endured.For now, Andrews appears focused on moving forward without allowing herself to carry blame for circumstances she could not control. Her openness about pregnancy loss also gives a more honest picture of the emotional realities that can exist behind a seemingly happy family life.
Article Summary: Erin Andrews and Jarret Stoll lost a pregnancy while trying to have another child. She and Stoll welcomed their son, Mack, in June 2023 after turning to surrogacy following a long fertility journey. During an appearance on Alex Cooper’s Call Her Daddy podcast, Andrews spoke about the pregnancy loss.

A heartwarming story about Travis Kelce buying a diner from his college days and turning it into a place that serves free meals to homeless people captured attention online. The tale sounded like the kind of quiet act of generosity fans might expect from the NFL star. But the emotional story does not hold up. Snopes investigated the claim and found no credible evidence that the diner, its owner or the alleged charity operation ever existed.The viral story began circulating online in June 2025, with social media posts claiming Kelce had purchased a small diner that once allowed him to eat without paying immediately while he was in college.One widely shared post described the supposed transformation in striking terms:According to the story, Kelce had regularly visited a diner run by a woman named Elena. She allegedly allowed the future NFL star to keep a running tab for two years. Years later, the story claimed, Kelce found Elena after learning that she was closing the business.The supposed reunion was presented as the emotional heart of the story. Kelce allegedly bought the diner and asked Elena to return to the kitchen, this time to prepare free meals for 120 homeless people each day.It was an appealing narrative, but the details could not be independently verified.Snopes reported that searches across major search engines found no credible news reports confirming that Kelce had purchased such a business or launched a daily meal program. Searches also failed to locate Kansas City establishments called Elena's Diner or Elena's Kitchen.That absence matters. A project involving an NFL star of Kelce's profile and free meals for more than 100 people every day would likely have generated some reliable coverage.The story gained extra attention because posts included photographs that appeared to show Kelce personally serving food to people experiencing homelessness. However, those images raised another major red flag.Snopes said an AI image detection service identified the photographs as highly likely to have been generated using artificial intelligence. The images reportedly contained visual inconsistencies, including unusual eyes and an oddly formed hand.The questionable photographs added to the evidence that the story was not a genuine account of Kelce's charitable work.Snopes also found another similar story claiming Kelce had donated $50,000 to a diner that supposedly fed him as a teenager. That version was likewise presented without credible evidence.The recurring pattern is important. Inspirational celebrity stories can spread rapidly because they offer a simple emotional message: someone who received kindness eventually returned it on a much larger scale. But an uplifting story is not automatically a true one.In this case, the evidence points in the opposite direction. The viral claim that, according to Snopes' investigation.Fans may still admire Kelce's real charitable efforts, but those should not be confused with an invented diner story simply because the narrative sounds believable.
Article Summary: Viral story about Travis Kelce buying a diner from his college days and turning it into a place that serves free meals to homeless people captured attention online. Snopes investigated the claim and found no credible evidence that the diner, its owner or the alleged charity operation ever existed.

T20I career so far

Abhishek Sharma has come a long way from the little boy in Amritsar who first picked up a cricket bat at the age of three-and-a-half. On his birthday, his journey stands out as one of the most remarkable rises in modern T20 cricket, from a promising youngster in Punjab to an India regular and the holder of the highest-ever ICC T20I batting rating.Abhishek's father, Raj Kumar Sharma, a former cricketer, introduced him to the game when he was just three-and-a-half. The youngster quickly developed an obsession with batting and progressed through Punjab's age-group system.His numbers soon began attracting attention. During the 2015-16 Vijay Merchant Trophy, Abhishek scored more than 1,200 runs at an average of 109.09 and also claimed 57 wickets. He captained Punjab to the Under-19 Asia Cup title in 2016 before becoming part of India's victorious Under-19 World Cup campaign in 2018.The IPL came at just 17, when Delhi Daredevils picked him in the 2018 auction. His career, however, did not explode immediately. Abhishek spent several seasons developing his game through domestic cricket and the IPL before finding the perfect platform for his aggressive style.A major influence during that period was Yuvraj Singh. The former India all-rounder became Abhishek's mentor and worked closely with him, particularly during the Covid-19 lockdown.Yuvraj understood the youngster's attacking instincts and encouraged him to embrace them rather than become overly cautious. That philosophy eventually became the foundation of Abhishek's T20 game.His international breakthrough came after making his T20I debut in July 2024. In February 2025, Abhishek produced one of the most devastating T20I innings by an Indian batter when he smashed 135 off just 54 balls against England in Mumbai. The innings contained 13 sixes and a 37-ball century, announcing him as one of India's most dangerous T20 batters.The 135 was only the beginning. During the 2025 Asia Cup, Abhishek established himself as India's attacking force at the top of the order. He scored 314 runs in seven matches at a strike rate of 200 and was named Player of the Tournament as India won the competition.His performances pushed him to the top of the ICC T20I batting rankings and eventually into record-breaking territory. After scoring 61 against Sri Lanka, Abhishek reached 931 rating points, the highest-ever rating achieved by a men's T20I batter.He surpassed Dawid Malan's previous record of 919 and moved beyond the best ratings achieved by India's Suryakumar Yadav and Virat Kohli.The numbers behind Abhishek's rise were extraordinary. In 2025, he became the first player to score more than 1,000 runs in T20 cricket in a calendar year while maintaining a strike rate above 200. He finished the year at a strike rate of 202 and smashed 108 sixes.His IPL performances were equally destructive. Playing for Sunrisers Hyderabad, Abhishek produced a stunning 141 off 55 balls against Punjab Kings in IPL 2025. He reached his fifty in only 16 balls and his century in 40, hitting 14 fours and 10 sixes as Hyderabad chased down 246. The innings broke KL Rahul's record for the highest score by an Indian batter in IPL history.His development has been shaped by several influential figures. Apart from Yuvraj, Abhishek has drawn lessons from players such as Shikhar Dhawan, Brian Lara and Travis Head. At Sunrisers, his partnership with Head showed how effectively his aggressive approach could work against the best bowling attacks.At the 2026 T20 World Cup, Abhishek added another major achievement to his growing list, playing a crucial role in India's title-winning campaign, including a blistering 52 off 21 balls in the final against New Zealand.Abhishek Sharma has played 56 T20Is between 2024 and 2026, scoring 1,629 runs in 55 innings at an average of 30.73 and a remarkable strike rate of 187.24. He has registered two centuries and 11 fifties, with a highest score of 135. His aggressive approach is reflected in his boundary count, with the left-hander hitting 164 fours and 104 sixes in his international career so far.
Article Summary: Abhishek Sharma started playing cricket at the age of three-and-a-half. His father, a former cricketer, introduced him to the game when he was just three. His international breakthrough came after making his T20I debut in July 2024. In February 2025, he smashed 135 off just 54 balls against England.

She broke former Indian women's captain Mithali Raj 's record of 10,868 runs. Mandhana also broke the record for most centuries (18) in international cricket, the most by any batter in the women's game, surpassing Meg Lanning and Laura Wolvaardt, who have 17 apiece. Mandhana has two hundreds in T20Is, two in Tests and 14 in ODIs. The elegant left-hander has 93 fifty-plus scores across formats in international cricket, the joint-most by any batter, alongside Raj.It was also Mandhana's second T20I hundred, thus making the 30-year-old the first Indian woman to score multiple centuries in the shortest format of the game.“I congratulate Smriti Mandhana on becoming the leading run-getter in women's internationals. I feel that it's high time that the national women's selection committee, led by Amita Sharma, appoints Smriti as the new captain in all three formats of the game. Harmanpreet Kaur can continue to play as a senior player in the side,” Edulji said while talking to TOI."Well deserved, Smriti! I’ve watched you grow from a young player into one of the finest batters India has produced. To see you go past my record and become the highest run-scorer in international cricket is a moment I’m genuinely proud of. Here’s to many more runs and milestones. Keep going!," posted Mithali on 'X' on Thursday.Under the 37-year-old Harmanpreet’s captaincy, the Women-in-Blue clinched their maiden ODI World Cup win last year, but exited in the group stage of the Women’s T20 World Cup for the second time in a row.However, they bounced back to beat England by 270 runs in the historic one-off Test at Lord’s. The national selectors have shown faith in Harmanpreet by retaining her as India’s captain for the ongoing Asia Cup in Dubai and the Asian Games in Japan in Sept.In an exclusive interview with TOI on July 14, Mandhana, when asked about whether she was ready for the India captaincy, replied by saying, “Yes, of course, I am ready!”After India’s league stage exit in the 2026 Women’s T20 World Cup, India's head coach Amol Muzumdar was asked about Harmanpreet's future, and he said he would like to see her continue as skipper. “It's up to the selectors to decide the captain. I think, yes, my short and sweet answer would be yes,” Muzumdar had stated.

NEW DELHI: Anshuman Hooda bursts into laughter when asked to choose between his office laptop and his cricket ball. “My cricket ball is my best friend,” he tells TimesofIndia.com.His elder brother, Vikram Hooda, says their mother, Prem Lata Singh, a primary class teacher at a Municipal Corporation of Delhi (MCD) school, is happy to see Anshuman pursue cricket, especially now that he has a stable job. “Earlier, they used to say that he needed a job. Now that he has one and is doing well, she is happy,” Vikram says of their parents.Anshuman had a breakout 2026 Delhi Premier League (DPL) season -- emerging as the Purple Cap winner with 22 scalps -- which played a crucial role in South Delhi Superstarz's title triumph.But there was a time when Hooda thought cricket had run its course. Two attempts at the Under-23 trials had gone by without success. There was no age-group cricket on his résumé, no traditional pathway through Delhi's junior system and no obvious route into first-class cricket. He had an engineering degree from Delhi Technological University (DTU) and a job at EY. The sensible thing, he thought, was to move on.“I tried for Under-23 for two years, but I couldn’t make it. I thought it would be very difficult because I hadn’t played any professional cricket or age-group cricket.It would have been very difficult to directly get selected for the Ranji Trophy or first-class cricket,” Anshuman recollects.“So at that time, I thought I should quit cricket and pursue my career in engineering or something.”But just when he thought of walking away from the game, his coach Harish Dagar, who runs a cricket academy named Delhi Cricket Hub in Delhi's Paschim Vihar, and trains youngsters at DTU, stepped up.“It was in 2023. He had just graduated. He had got the job through campus placement and was ready to move on with his life. I pleaded with him to give it one more year. I asked him to come to my academy four days a week for a year, and if nothing would pan out, I would let him pursue his corporate job,” reminisces Dagar.Then came the Delhi Premier League (DPL). And with it came a completely different possibility. For a young man who had arrived late to leather-ball cricket, DPL became the stage on which his raw pace, athleticism and appetite for fast bowling could finally be seen. The numbers followed. The attention followed, and now Anshuman is finally ready to become a full-time cricketer.“I have seen some substantial progress in my cricket in recent months and in this tournament. So in the coming times, I might shift my whole focus to cricket and give it my all,” he says.Anshuman is 25 and, in cricketing terminology, he can be called a late bloomer. But the most unusual thing about Anshuman's story is perhaps where it began. Not with a cricket academy. Not with a junior tournament. Not with a childhood obsession with bowling. With roller skates.Growing up, Anshuman was a national-level roller skater. Cricket existed around him, but it was not initially the sport that defined him. His elder brother Vikram had played cricket, and there was, as Anshuman puts it, a familiar sibling dynamic. His brother took science. He took science. His brother studied engineering. He studied engineering. But when it came to cricket, Anshuman's journey took its own route.It was only when he reached college that the game began to take hold.“I just started playing in college, and that’s when I got into leather-ball cricket professionally, playing for the college team and all. That’s when I fell in love with bowling fast, getting wickets and the aggression that comes with it. I just loved bowling fast.”That love became the starting point of something neither his résumé nor his previous sporting journey could have predicted.Harish Dagar first noticed Anshuman in 2019 while they were at university. What caught his eye was not a polished fast bowler. It was the physical package.Fitness. Arm speed. Natural movement.Anshuman was playing tennis-ball cricket when Dagar asked him to try medium pace. The first attempts were raw and erratic, but there was enough pace and athletic ability for the coach to believe there was something worth developing.“His body alignment was natural. His strength was natural, and his pace was natural. But he didn't have enough strength in his body initially. That's why I told him that if you don't maintain your fitness along with your natural pace, you will face problems," says Dagar.“He was also busy with his job. He couldn't always take proper sessions. He would come at night, then have to go to the gym and take practice sessions. It was very hectic.“I worked on his mind 80-85 per cent. I made him mentally strong. I told him never to think that he was tired or burdened.“Once I worked on his mindset and the roadmap was clear in front of him, he knew what he had to do. At one point he had to focus on fitness, at another he had to do his job, and then he had to come to me for his sessions."Anshuman graduated from DTU with a degree in Production and Industrial Engineering and joined a multinational company in 2023. He worked from home, which helped him juggle the demands of employment and an increasingly serious cricket career. But balancing the two was never going to be easy.Fast bowling is an unforgiving craft. It demands strength, recovery, repetition and hours of training. Dagar's approach was to build Anshuman patiently, focusing not merely on speed but on the physical and mental foundations that could allow him to bowl fast consistently.Anshuman also had to understand his own body. He had dealt with niggles and the physical toll that comes with repeatedly accelerating, landing and transferring his entire body weight through a bowling action.“Fast bowling is not a very comfortable activity for the body. You accelerate, then your whole body has to absorb the impact before you bowl. It definitely takes a toll on the body,” he says.But there was no great mystery behind his motivation. He adds: “It was just the love for the sport and the love for bowling fast that kept me motivated and helped me come back stronger every time.”That attitude has been central to his development.Dagar describes the next stage of the process in more professional terms: periodisation, rest, strength work, workload scheduling, diet, physiotherapy and technical skills. Anshuman had to develop a stock ball and variations such as the leg-cutter and off-cutter while ensuring that his body could cope with the demands of pace.The objective was never simply to produce a fast delivery. It was to produce a fast bowler. The first real crack in the wall came through the DPL.In 2024, he got his opportunity with South Delhi, initially finding chances hard to come by. Then came a spell that changed perceptions. The next season brought more opportunities, including a five-wicket haul, and soon IPL franchises were looking at him as a net bowler and trial candidate.The journey from someone contemplating quitting cricket to someone attracting franchise attention had happened remarkably quickly. For Anshuman, the attention became tangible when Shikhar Dhawan , the owner of his DPL team, spoke to him after his performances.“Shikhar Dhawan himself, the team owner, surprised me. He came and we had a little conversation. He gave me some very good tips and a direction to work towards from here,” he says.It was a moment of validation. For someone who had spent years outside the conventional cricket pathway, being noticed by an established name carried significance beyond a conversation.At 140 kmph, Anshuman possesses the one commodity that can change a fast bowler's career quickly: pace. Coach Dagar believes there is more to come. Anshuman is not shy about wanting it.“Definitely, speed is what I want. If I can, I will definitely look to bowl even faster and build the strength and skills to do that, while making sure there is no compromise on accuracy and line,” said Anshuman.That final clause is important. Pace can attract attention. Accuracy keeps a fast bowler in a team. For Anshuman, the next challenge is therefore not simply touching a bigger number on the speed gun. It is learning how to sustain high pace across long spells, particularly in red-ball cricket.He is already thinking about it. “These are the things we prepare for. Who bowls in a four-day or five-day game and bowls long spells with the same effort? That is what I am preparing for. If I get an opportunity, I will definitely do that.”Anshuman's ambition is clear. First, Delhi. Then first-class cricket. Then, eventually, IPL and India.“The eventual goal is to play and win matches for the country. That is my ultimate goal,” he says.There is, however, one more conversation happening in Anshuman's life. The conversation between security and possibility. An engineering degree and a job at a good company offer a predictable future. And he has got a promotion before the start of the DPL season as well. Cricket offers something very different: uncertainty, competition and the possibility of a career that can disappear as quickly as it arrives.For now, Anshuman has returned to work. But his cricket has progressed to the point where continuing to divide himself between the two may no longer be possible.“Currently, I have joined back. But as I have seen some substantial progress in my cricket in recent months and in this tournament, I might, in the coming times, shift my whole focus to cricket and give it my all.”It is a significant sentence from someone who once thought about quitting the sport altogether. There is also a quiet irony in the fact that the engineer who learned to manage competing demands may soon have to choose one.Anshuman knows where he wants to go.“I will give it my all. Argentina began paying tribute to Lionel Messi after the football great announced his retirement from international football earlier this week.The first tribute came during the Copa Argentina match between Velez Sarsfield and Boca Juniors on Wednesday, when play was stopped in the 10th minute for a round of applause at the Estadio Mario Alberto Kempes.Fans across the stadium stood and applauded Messi, bringing the game to a halt for a brief moment.Two of Messi's former Argentina teammates, Leandro Paredes and Manuel Lanzini, were on the pitch during the tribute.The match later ended 0-0, with Boca Juniors winning the penalty shootout 4-3.The tribute follows a decision by the Argentine Football Association, which announced that referees will stop play in the 10th minute of every match in the upcoming round of the Clausura tournament, as well as in other men's and women's competitions across the country, to honour Messi's international career.Messi announced his international retirement after the 2026 FIFA World Cup, ending a career that lasted 21 years with the Argentina team.He finished with 125 goals and 68 assists in 207 appearances for Argentina.In his retirement message, Messi said the decision "hurts the depths of my soul", but added that he "knows the time has come" to stop representing his country.Messi's biggest achievement with Argentina came when he led the team to the 2022 FIFA World Cup title in Qatar.He also helped Argentina win the Copa America in 2021 and 2024, ending the country's 28-year wait for a major trophy.Although he is one of Argentina's biggest sporting icons, Messi has never played club football professionally in his home country. Article Title: “My cup for myself was half empty”: How LeBron James’ wife Savannah James rediscovered herself after motherhood and built a life beyond raising her three children
Article Text:
How LeBron James’ wife Savannah James rediscovered herself after motherhood and built a life beyond raising her three children(Image via Getty Images)

Savannah James rediscovered herself while building a life beyond motherhood

Everybody’s Crazy

A new chapter took shape as Savannah James built a life beyond motherhood

Let It Break

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Savannah James spent much of her adult life putting family first. She became a mother at 18 and eventually raised three children while LeBron James built a historic NBA career. Yet behind the polished family image, Savannah has admitted that she struggled with her own identity. Years of being a mother and wife had left little room to ask a simple question: who was Savannah outside those roles?That question became harder to ignore as the children grew older. Savannah eventually started taking time for herself and exploring interests beyond family life. What followed was a gradual shift that brought new projects, business ventures and a better understanding of what she needed personally.Savannah James welcomed Bronny James in October 2004, followed by Bryce in June 2007 and Zhuri in October 2014. With three children at different stages of life and LeBron James constantly balancing an NBA schedule, much of Savannah’s attention naturally went toward her family.Still, Savannah later acknowledged that the balance had become difficult. During a 2025 episode of, the podcast Savannah co-hosts with April McDaniel, she spoke openly about feeling disconnected from the person she had been before motherhood. “It wasn’t just my kids, it was my husband, I felt like I didn’t have an identity outside of that,” Savannah said during the podcast.She also explained how much of her energy went into being a mother.“I was too wrapped up in just being their mom,” Savannah said in the same conversation. That realization forced her to look beyond the responsibilities that had defined much of her life.Savannah described the feeling in even more personal terms during the 2025 podcast discussion. “My cup for myself was half empty,” she said.The answer was not to step away from her children or marriage. Instead, Savannah began creating small pockets of time that belonged only to her. She recalled taking solo weekend trips while living in Ohio and learning to become more protective of her schedule.“I hate to say it like this, but just be selfish with my time,” Savannah said on Everybody’s Crazy in 2025. She also explained that she needed to discover who she was outside of Bronny and Bryce. That process had roots several years earlier.Savannah had already discussed the emotional weight of balancing family and personal needs before that 2025 conversation. In a June 21, 2024 interview with “Harper’s Bazaar”, she talked about creatingwith April McDaniel, a platform focused on women, personal growth and self-discovery.The idea connected directly to Savannah’s own experience. She wanted women to have space to slow down and think about themselves instead of constantly meeting everyone else’s needs.“If I’m working from a glass half empty, I’m not good to anybody,” Savannah said on June 21, 2024.That mindset also shaped the way Savannah approached motherhood as her children became more independent. Bronny moved into college basketball, Bryce continued developing his own basketball career, and Zhuri grew into her own interests. Savannah suddenly had more room to explore what came next.She used that space to build a public identity separate from LeBron James. Alongside “Everybody’s Crazy”, Savannah developed business ventures and continued working on projects connected to wellness, lifestyle and personal growth. In 2025, she also launched Reframe, a skincare brand that added another piece to her growing business portfolio.The change did not mean Savannah stopped being a mother. It meant motherhood no longer had to be the only role defining her. After years of giving most of her energy to LeBron James and their three children, Savannah began treating her own ambitions as something worth protecting too. Her journey shows a quieter side of family life that rarely appears in the spotlight: sometimes finding yourself starts with simply making enough room to hear your own thoughts again.

She became a mother at 18 and eventually raised three children while LeBron James built a historic NBA career. After years of giving most of her energy to LeBron James and their three children, Savannah began treating her ambitions as something too.

Article Title: 'Serving country against biological clock': Spain to fund egg freezing for women footballers; what does it mean?
Article Text:
Mariona Caldentey, Irene Paredes, Alexia Putellas, Claudia Pina and Olga Carmona look on during a training session at RCDE Stadium on June 02, 2025 in Barcelona, Spain. (Photo/Getty Images)

Players raised the issue with the federation

What egg freezing means for elite athletes

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

No clear rules yet in women's football

Spain's football federation is preparing to pay for egg-freezing procedure for its leading women footballers, in a move aimed at helping players balance motherhood with careers at the highest level.According to a report by EL Pais, the Royal Spanish Football Federation (RFEF) is finalising an agreement with a fertility clinic that will allow members of the Spain women's team to undergo egg vitrification. The agreement is expected to be announced later this month, while discussions continue over the exact terms and costs.The move comes as more women athletes face the challenge of fitting pregnancy into long sporting careers. A football career can continue into a player's thirties, but pregnancy often means several months away from training and competition, and returning to the highest level can be difficult.Former Spain captain Alexia Putellas said the team's captains had discussed the issue with the federation and welcomed the proposal."The federation understands that you are serving your country against your biological clock, that you cannot stop and cannot be a mother because you need your body to work," Putellas was quoted as saying by EL Pais."The group of captains had a concern because it is very important for a player to experience World Cups, but that means that those of us who have the desire to become mothers do not find it easy to fit it in."The federation has not yet confirmed whether it will cover the full treatment, only the egg preservation process, or also the egg retrieval procedure.Sports medicine specialist Eva Ferrer said egg vitrification has become a topic of discussion in women's football only over the past couple of years.She explained that there is still limited research on how ovarian stimulation affects athletes. "There are not enough studies on how the treatment [ovarian stimulation] could affect, for example, the joints or soft tissue," Ferrer said as quoted by EL Pais.She added that training may need to be adjusted during treatment to reduce the risk of injury. She also said the medications used during the process must be declared through a Therapeutic Use Exemption (TUE) so athletes do not face anti-doping issues.The treatment usually lasts about two weeks. During that period, the player injects hormonal medication to stimulate the ovaries so multiple eggs mature instead of one. Doctors then retrieve the eggs through a procedure performed under sedation.After the procedure, players may experience bleeding, discomfort, swelling, fluid retention, migraines and lower energy levels while the ovaries recover. Clinics generally recommend collecting around 10 oocytes, though the process can be repeated if needed.Gynecologist Rebeca Beguería said elite athletes do not return to peak physical condition immediately after treatment."The medical protocol states that normal life can be resumed, but for a high-performance athlete these are days when you do not perform at the same level: you will not run as fast or at the same intensity," she told EL Pais.She added that players face a greater risk of injury and abdominal damage during recovery."Your body's blood is redistributed; it is concentrated there; the abdomen and chest are more swollen, there is a tendency to migraines and fluid retention."Beguería also pointed out that while egg freezing helps players delay pregnancy, it does not remove the medical risks associated with becoming pregnant at an older age."Medically, the recommendation is that women get pregnant as early as possible, because biologically we are designed to be mothers by, at most, age 35 and we have extended that."The proposal has also highlighted the lack of regulations around fertility treatment in professional women's football.Lawyer Tania Tejeira wrote in an opinion piece in Palco23 that neither FIFA nor UEFA currently has a specific protocol covering treatments such as egg freezing or other assisted reproductive technologies, despite more players choosing these options.At present, the main international guidance comes from the World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA), which requires medications used during fertility treatment to be reviewed and, where necessary, approved through a Therapeutic Use Exemption.
Article Summary: Spain's football federation is preparing to pay for egg-freezing procedure for its leading women footballers. Move aimed at helping players balance motherhood with careers at the highest level. Agreement expected to be announced later this month, while discussions continue over the exact terms and costs.

Article Title: 2 NDMC staffers killed as Thar rams bike from behind in Delhi Cantt
Article Text:
Two New Delhi Municipal Council employees died after a speeding SUV hit their motorcycle (Representative image)





NEW DELHI: Two New Delhi Municipal Council (NDMC) employees were killed after a Mahindra Thar hit the motorcycle they were on from behind in Delhi Cantonment Wednesday evening.The driver of the SUV, who is also its owner and was allegedly driving rashly, was arrested.Sukhbir and Anju, both in their forties, were co-workers and Group D employees. Anju was part of the civic organisation's nursing staff and Sukhbir worked as a painter. The two were returning to their houses in the same locality of Dwarka Sector 1 after finishing work at NDMC's office on Lodhi Road."The accident took place around 5 pm. A staff member of Delhi Cantt police station, who was returning from duty, noticed that the bike was hit near the IOC Red Light and immediately alerted the police station," a senior police officer said.A team of cops reached the spot and rushed Sukhbir and Anju to a nearby hospital, where doctors declared them dead.Bhupendra, the 26-year-old Thar driver, is a resident of Jhajjar in Haryana and owns a milk booth in Rohini. Locals caught him after the accident and handed him over to police, who arrested him.A case was registered at Delhi Cantt police station under Sections 281 (rash driving or riding on a public way) and 106 (death due to negligence) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS).Rohit, Anju's son, told TOI, "My mother had been working as a nursing staff officer with NDMC since 2007. It was largely because of her income that my two siblings and I were able to complete our schooling. She followed the same routine every day: she would leave home around 8 am and take a bus to work. On her way back, Sukhbir would drop her home as they both lived in the same locality."Recalling the moment when things fell apart Wednesday evening, Rohit said, "I received a call informing me that my mother had met with an accident. When I reached the spot, I found that she had succumbed to her injuries. The driver was speeding and deserves the harshest punishment. We want justice for my mother."Chote Lal, Sukhbir's elder brother, said he got to know about the accident after trying to reach him. "I kept calling him. Finally, a cop picked up the phone to tell me that he had died in the accident. It was just him and me in our family, no one else. I want justice."
Article Summary: Sukhbir and Anju, both in their forties, were co-workers and Group D employees. Anju was part of the civic organisation's nursing staff and Sukhbir worked as a painter. The driver of the SUV, who is also its owner and was allegedly driving rashly, was arrested.

Article Title: A fellowship, Miranda House and the making of Gloria Steinem
Article Text:
Gloria Steinem's early year in India profoundly shaped her understanding of feminism and activism.





Gloria Steinem was 22. Having graduated from Smith College, she received a Chester Bowles Asian Fellowship that gave her the chance to spend a year in India. Long after, the journalist, activist and feminist said it was in India that she began to understand feminism without yet knowing the word for it.Steinem, who became one of the most recognisable faces of the American women’s movement for more than five decades, died Wednesday at 92.Steinem lived for about a year in Miranda House hostel in Delhi, according to the college principal. She then travelled to Calcutta, southern India and Bombay, wrote about the country, and learnt grassroots organising from the followers of Mahatma Gandhi.The trip to India, she is said to have recounted later, appealed to her not merely as a chance to step away from the life she knew, but as a way of discovering for herself a country whose history and culture had long interested her. Steinem even featured in sari ads, as a way of supplementing her income in India .In 2014, she told Rajya Sabha TV that she was struck by the role women had played in India’s Independence movement and by women’s struggles against oppressive practices. Women such as Kamaladevi Chattopadhyay showed her a history of female activism she had not enco­untered in United States. “I didn’t know what feminism was,” she said in the interview.Miranda House principal professor Bijayalaxmi Nanda said Steinem visited the college twice and remained closely connected to her memories of the institution. During a visit around 2014 with economist Devaki Jain, Steinem spoke about how her time at Miranda House had helped her forge friendships with women, and influenced her engagement with social justice and equality.“She consistently spoke about women’s rights in the workplace and society, bodily autonomy, and was a strong voice against child trafficking and pornography. When she visited, she spoke about how the college had transformed her life and how she had made many women friends here,” Nanda said.The experience stayed with her. “I was here 18 years ago for almost two years. I came to like India very much and to feel influenced by India very much,” Steinem reportedly told India Today in 1976.In 2011, she told the then Asia Society president, “Going to India helped me enormously because I didn’t learn as much as I should have here. For instance, I didn’t understand Dalit culture. At the time, Dalits were still being referred to as ‘untouchables’. I was deeply affected.”Steinem became a leading figure of second-wave feminism, campaigning for reproductive rights, equal pay, an end to domestic violence and greater political representation. She helped found New York magazine, co-founded Women’s Action Alliance, and helped establish National Women’s Political Caucus. Her most enduring journalistic contribution was Ms. magazine, launched in 1971 as an insert in New York magazine before becoming independent the following year.On Steinem’s 90th birthday two years ago, Miranda House college marked the occasion with women’s rights and anti-trafficking activist Ruchira Gupta and announced a Gloria Steinem Travel Grant for work on gender issues. Though the grant has not yet been used, Nanda said the college may now revive it in Steinem’s memory. “We will also plan a conference or some event so that the present generation knows about her contributions and what she stood for,” she said.
Article Summary: Gloria Steinem lived for about a year in Miranda House hostel in Delhi, according to the college principal. She then travelled to Calcutta, southern India and Bombay, wrote about the country, and learnt grassroots organising from the followers of Mahatma Gandhi.

Article Title: In 1978, Richard Branson bought a bare 74-acre Caribbean island for $180,000; it now shelters more than 140 animal species, including breeding lemurs and giant tortoises
Article Text:
An aerial view of Necker Island in the British Virgin Islands, a private island in the Caribbean. Credits - Wikimedia Commons

A reluctant purchase becomes a passion

Building a home for species with nowhere else to go

The Great House on Necker Island, built after Hurricane Irene. Credits - Wikipedia

A sanctuary that sustains itself

In 1978, Richard Branson, then 28, paid $180,000 for a small, uninhabited island in the British Virgin Islands. Necker Island had no fresh water source, no buildings and barely any vegetation beyond scrub and cactus. Nearly fifty years after the purchase, and roughly four decades since the resort itself was completed, that same 74-acre island supports a working conservation programme that shelters well over 140 species, several of which now breed there naturally, including lemurs from Madagascar and giant tortoises from the Seychelles.Branson has told the story of the purchase many times over the years, and the details rarely change. According to an account he has given describing the negotiation, he first visited the British Virgin Islands on a trip meant to impress a woman he was pursuing at the time, having been offered a free look at the islands by a realtor who did not realise how little money Branson actually had. The asking price for Necker was around six million dollars, far beyond what he could afford at the time, running an eight-year-old record label, so Branson made an opening offer of just $100,000.The seller turned him down at first but came back a year later, still unable to find a buyer, and eventually accepted a revised offer of $180,000. At that point he owned essentially raw land, with no infrastructure, and the sale came with a condition that he build a resort on the site within four years. Turning that bare ground into something worth visiting took nearly a decade and set the pattern for what followed: a slow, deliberate transformation rather than a quick development.The wildlife did not arrive all at once, and it was introduced deliberately. Over the decades since the resort was completed, Branson and his team have deliberately introduced species that were struggling in their native ranges, choosing Necker specifically because its isolation from the mainland makes it easier to protect animals from predators and disease, even though the island itself operates as a small, tightly controlled private resort where guest access to the animals is limited and managed by the conservation team. As Branson explains in a PBS documentary filmed on the island, lemurs have become one of what he calls the island's flagship conservation species, brought in after habitat loss in Madagascar left many of their relatives fighting for survival at home. Giant tortoises, native to the Aldabra atoll in the Seychelles, followed a similar path, arriving as part of a breeding programme rather than as a decorative addition to the grounds. Flamingos, macaws, iguanas and a rotating cast of other species have joined them, each one added with the specific aim of giving vulnerable animals a secure place to establish new populations. That patient approach appears to be paying off in the way conservationists actually measure success, through births rather than just headcounts.Today, the tortoises in particular have reached a milestone that is rare in captive conservation work, breeding naturally on the island rather than relying on animals shipped in from elsewhere to maintain their numbers. The breeding success became especially significant in 2021, when the island recorded its first Aldabra giant tortoise hatchlings. The young animals were discovered soon after emerging from their nests and were monitored by the island's conservation team to make sure they remained healthy. The event showed that the tortoises were not simply surviving in an introduced population but were completing an important part of their life cycle on Necker itself. The island's wildlife programme has followed a similar approach with other species, creating conditions in which animals can establish themselves rather than simply being displayed for visitors. Virgin Limited Edition now describes Necker as a natural breeding ground for several rare species, including Madagascan lemurs, giant tortoises, rock lizards and flamingos.A dedicated wildlife team now manages the island's animal population full time, treating Necker less like a private garden and more like a functioning sanctuary with its own breeding programmes and veterinary oversight. Branson himself has framed it in exactly those terms in his own public comments, describing a personal commitment to protecting disappearing species that has clearly outlasted his initial reasons for buying the place at all. Necker Island remains one of a small number of personal purchases from that era that developed decades later into an active conservation programme.
Article Summary: Richard Branson bought Necker Island in 1978 for just $180,000. The 74-acre island now supports a working conservation programme. It shelters well over 140 species, including lemurs from Madagascar and giant tortoises from the Seychelles. A dedicated wildlife team manages the island's population full time.
